issues.legal_issue: A municipal authority may not convert a public park into a commercial complex where doing so destroys the park’s public and environmental functions.
material_facts: The park was an old, historically important public open space and the only park in a heavily congested commercial and residential area.
Construction of the underground shopping complex involved cutting trees and made further planting impossible, changing the character of the park.
The municipal authority had an obligatory duty to maintain parks and plant trees, but no proper study of local conditions was undertaken before the project was approved.
The stated aim of reducing congestion was not supported by the project; the court found the complex would increase congestion and pollution.
issues.conclusion: The commercial construction violated the municipal authority’s duties and the public trust doctrine; the authority could not sacrifice the park’s public and environmental functions for the project.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959, the municipal authority had duties to maintain parks, plant trees, protect the environment, and provide urban amenities. The public trust doctrine, recognized as part of Indian law in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) 1 SCC 388, prevents a public authority entrusted with public resources from diverting them to restricted private benefit. The Court also relied on Article 21 and the principles concerning public open spaces in Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577.

predicates.municipal_action_challenged: A person challenges a public authority’s decision concerning the use of a public park.
predicates.public_park_used_for_commercial_construc: The public authority permits commercial construction on land maintained as a public park.
predicates.park_public_or_environmental_functions_d: The construction prevents the park from continuing to provide its established public or environmental functions.
predicates.park_ecological_harm_increased: The construction increases environmental harm associated with the park or its surroundings.

issues.definition: When a challenged public decision uses a park for commercial construction that destroys its public or environmental functions or increases ecological harm, the conversion is unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: A municipality cannot validly delegate its statutory decision-making powers or enter into a contract disposing of municipal property without complying with mandatory procedures.
material_facts: The municipal body created a High Power Committee and purported to give it authority to dispose of municipal property and settle agreement terms.
The project was not properly listed for consideration at the relevant meetings, and the body approved it without supporting proposals, plans, feasibility material, or an informed discussion.
The agreement allowed the builder to construct a permanent complex, recover its costs and profit, retain control for an indefinite period, and lease shops on the municipality’s behalf.
The agreement was not executed as required by law, and the required approval of the State Government for the project was not obtained.
The court found that the arrangement in substance transferred an interest in municipal property, despite being framed as a licence and construction arrangement.
issues.conclusion: The delegation and approval process breached mandatory statutory requirements, and the agreement was invalid and not binding on the municipal authority.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 119 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959, governed notice of business and delegation of functions. Sections 128 and 129 governed disposal of municipal property; Sections 131 to 133 governed municipal contracts and their execution; and Section 136 required approval of the project by the State Government in the circumstances found by the Court. A statutory body must follow the manner prescribed by statute. The Court relied on Dr. H.S. Rikhy v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, AIR 1962 SC 554, for strict compliance with mandatory statutory requirements and the absence of estoppel against a statute. It also relied on Chawalier I.I. Iyappan v. Dharmodayam Company, (1963) 1 SCR 85, in considering the licence arrangement and its revocation.

rule.if: municipal_property_transaction_challenged and (statutory_decision_powers_delegated_without_authority or required_meeting_procedure_not_followed or transaction_substantially_disposes_of_property_interest) and mandatory_contract_requirements_unmet

predicates.municipal_property_transaction_challenge: A party challenges a public body's agreement concerning municipal property.
predicates.statutory_decision_powers_delegated_with: The public body gives a committee or person decision-making powers that the governing law does not permit it to delegate.
predicates.required_meeting_procedure_not_followed: The public body considers or approves the transaction without following the required notice and meeting process.
predicates.transaction_substantially_disposes_of_pr: The agreement gives another person substantial control or use of public property, regardless of the label attached to the arrangement.
predicates.mandatory_contract_requirements_unmet: The agreement is made without complying with mandatory requirements governing approval or execution of public contracts.

issues.definition: A challenged municipal property transaction is invalid and not binding when statutory powers are improperly delegated, required meeting procedures are bypassed, or the transaction disposes of a property interest without mandatory contractual compliance.

issues.legal_issue: Development of land in a designated development area without the required written permission is unlawful even when the developer has municipal approval.
material_facts: The project involved construction beneath land in an area declared a development area.
The builder undertook the project as a principal, not as an agent carrying out development on behalf of the municipal authority.
The development authority had not sanctioned the building plan; its involvement was limited to a layout plan, and sanctioned drawings were unavailable.
The builder proceeded with construction despite the absence of the required development permission.
issues.conclusion: The construction was illegal because the required permission under the development legislation had not been obtained.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, required written permission from the Vice-Chairman for development in a declared development area and required development to accord with applicable plans. The Court applied the definition of development in Section 2(e) and distinguished development by a private principal from work undertaken by a public authority through an agent.

predicates.development_area_construction_challenged: A party challenges construction or other development in an area subject to development controls.
predicates.private_developer_carries_out_developmen: A private developer carries out the development for its own project rather than as an agent of the public authority.
predicates.required_written_development_permission_: The developer has not obtained the required written permission from the competent development authority.

issues.definition: When a private developer carries out development in a controlled area without the required written permission, the development is unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority’s award of a valuable public-property project without competition is invalid when the process is arbitrary, unfair, or unsupported by public interest.
material_facts: The project concerned valuable municipal land and offered the builder substantial commercial benefits under a one-sided agreement.
No tenders were invited, no project or feasibility report was obtained, and the authority did not assess whether other builders could offer equally competent work on better terms.
The project was approved without an informed examination of its costs or effects, and the stated congestion-reduction purpose was contradicted by the likely increase in congestion.
The court found that the process had been used to confer an undue benefit on the builder rather than to serve the public interest.
issues.conclusion: The award and agreement were arbitrary, unreasonable, and contrary to public interest; the absence of tenders was unjustified in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Public property must be dealt with for public interest and in a manner consistent with fairness and reasonableness. Public auction or tenders are ordinary means of securing that interest, although departure is possible for rational, non-discriminatory reasons. Judicial review may intervene for illegality, procedural violation, irrationality, arbitrariness, or mala fides. The Court relied on Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) 3 SCC 489; Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir (1980) 4 SCC 1; Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal (1987) 2 SCC 295; Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) 6 SCC 651; and G.B. Mahajan v. Jalgaon Municipal Council (1991) 3 SCC 91.

rule.if: public_project_award_challenged and valuable_public_property_transferred and no_competitive_process_used and no_rational_public_interest_reason_for_departure and (one_sided_private_benefit or decision_made_without_informed_assessment)

predicates.public_project_award_challenged: A party challenges a public authority’s decision to award a project or deal with public property.
predicates.valuable_public_property_transferred: The project gives a private person substantial use or control of valuable public property.
predicates.no_competitive_process_used: The authority awards the project without a tender, auction, or comparable competitive process.
predicates.no_rational_public_interest_reason_for_d: The authority has no rational, non-discriminatory public-interest justification for not using a competitive process.
predicates.one_sided_private_benefit: The transaction gives the private recipient substantial benefits while leaving the public authority with inadequate control or protection.
predicates.decision_made_without_informed_assessmen: The authority decides without adequate evaluation of the project’s costs, feasibility, alternatives, or public effects.

issues.definition: An award concerning valuable public property is arbitrary and invalid when it is made without competition, lacks a rational public-interest justification, and confers one-sided private benefit or follows no informed assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A public body is not estopped from changing its position when its earlier position supported an action that was contrary to law.
material_facts: The municipal authority initially supported the project and appealed against the High Court judgment, but later withdrew its appeals and supported that judgment.
The builder relied on the authority’s earlier position to argue that it could not change its stance.
The Court found that the project and agreement contravened statutory requirements and were against public interest.
issues.conclusion: The municipal authority was not estopped from changing its position because estoppel cannot require a public body to maintain an unlawful action.
issues.legal_principle: A public body cannot be held to an earlier position when doing so would perpetuate conduct contrary to statute. The Court distinguished Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd. (1968) 2 SCR 366 and The Ganges Manufacturing Co. v. Sourujmull (1880) ILR Cal 669, and relied on the principle in Dr. H.S. Rikhy v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, AIR 1962 SC 554, that there is no estoppel against a statute.

predicates.public_body_position_challenged: A party argues that a public body must adhere to a position it took earlier in the dispute.
predicates.public_body_previously_supported_action: The public body previously supported or pursued the action that is now challenged.
predicates.earlier_action_contrary_to_law: The action previously supported by the public body is found to contravene governing law.

issues.definition: A public body that previously supported an unlawful action is not estopped from changing its position to correct that action.

issues.legal_issue: Equitable considerations do not justify preserving unlawful commercial construction, though a portion may be retained when it serves a distinct public duty.
material_facts: The builder proceeded under an interim order that expressly placed the construction at its own risk and barred a claim to equity if the appeals failed.

The construction was substantially complete, but the court found it unlawful and likely to increase congestion and pollution; the builder and prospective allottees sought relief based on their investments and interests.
One block could be converted to a parking facility, and the municipal authority had a duty to provide and maintain parking lots.
The court ordered demolition of the other three blocks and restoration of the park, while directing that the parking block be converted and operated as a parking lot.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected relief that would preserve the unlawful shopping complex, ordered demolition of the commercial blocks and restoration of the park, but retained one block for public parking and directed the municipal authority to complete and maintain that use.
issues.legal_principle: Courts should not use equitable discretion to encourage or perpetuate illegal construction; unauthorized construction that cannot be regularized must be removed. The Court relied on K. Ramadas Shenoy v. Chief Officers, Town Municipal Council, Udipi (1975) 1 SCR 680; Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577; Pleasant Stay Hotel v. Palani Hills Conservation Council (1995) 6 SCC 127; Cantonment Board, Jabalpur v. S.N. Awasthi (1995) Supp. 4 SCC 595; Pratibha Cooperative Housing Society v. State of Maharashtra (1991) 3 SCC 341; and Dr. G.N. Khajuria v. Delhi Development Authority (1995) 5 SCC 762. Section 114 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959, also made provision for parking lots an obligatory municipal duty, which supported retaining the parking component.

rule.if: illegal_public_construction_challenged and construction_proceeded_at_builder_risk and (continued_use_would_harm_public_space_or_environment or construction_cannot_be_regularized) and distinct_component_can_serve_obligatory_public_need

predicates.illegal_public_construction_challenged: A party challenges construction on public land that the court finds unlawful.
predicates.construction_proceeded_at_builder_risk: The builder continues construction despite being informed that it proceeds at its own risk.
predicates.continued_use_would_harm_public_space_or: Continued use of the construction would impair public space or worsen environmental or local conditions.
predicates.construction_cannot_be_regularized: The unlawful construction cannot lawfully be allowed to remain in its existing use.
predicates.distinct_component_can_serve_obligatory_: A separable part of the construction can be adapted to meet a distinct public need for which the public authority is responsible.

issues.definition: When unlawful construction cannot be regularized and its continued use harms public space or the environment, it is removed and the public space restored, while a separable component may be retained for a distinct public need.
